lessons.title: Sourcing and Preparing Local Scrap Steel for the Forge
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 9, Lesson 1 of the Yok and Pan Blacksmith training. In this lesson we focus on the single most important input for your business: raw material. In many African markets, virgin steel is expensive and often imported, but scrap steel is abundant and cheap. Your ability to identify, sort, and prepare scrap steel determines your product quality, your fuel efficiency, and your profit margin. We will work through practical steps you can apply today in your own workshop. First, understand the types of scrap you will encounter. Vehicle leaf springs are excellent for knives, machetes, and heavy tools because they are usually medium to high carbon steel. Coil springs from trucks and cars are also good, though they are harder to straighten. Rebar is common but often low carbon and soft; it is better for decorative work, hooks, and non-cutting tools. Old files and rashers are high carbon and make excellent knives and chisels. Bearings, shafts, and plough discs are also valuable. Avoid galvanized steel, painted steel, and anything with chrome plating because the fumes are toxic and the coating ruins forge welds. When you collect scrap, carry a small magnet and a file. The magnet tells you if the steel is ferrous. The file tells you about hardness: if the file bites easily, the steel is soft; if it skates, the steel is hard. You can also use the spark test on a grinding wheel. Low carbon steel gives long yellow sparks with few bursts. High carbon steel gives short bright sparks with many star-like bursts. Practice this until you can sort by eye and by spark. Next, establish a buying system. Do not rely on chance. Build relationships with mechanics, welders, construction sites, and scrap dealers. Offer a fair price per kilogram and pay promptly. Keep a simple notebook with the date, source, weight, type, and price. This record helps you calculate your true cost per finished piece. In many African cities, scrap prices fluctuate, so buy in bulk when prices are low and store material under a roof to prevent rust. Rust is not fatal, but heavy rust wastes metal and time. For storage, sort by type and size. Keep leaf springs in one pile, files in another, and rebar in a third. Label each pile with a painted mark or a wooden tag. This saves time when you start a job. Before forging, prepare the steel. Cut pieces to length with a hacksaw or a cut-off wheel. Remove dirt, grease, and paint with a wire brush or by burning in a fire outside the forge. Never burn galvanized or painted metal inside your workshop. If you must use coated steel, do the cleaning outdoors with a mask and good ventilation. For leaf springs, anneal them first if you need to drill or cut. Annealing means heating to a dull red and cooling slowly in ash or sand. This softens the steel and saves your drill bits. For files, do not anneal unless you plan to re-harden them; instead, grind the teeth off before forging to avoid cold shuts. When you forge, start with a clean fire. Use charcoal or coal that is free of stones and excessive dust. A clean fire gives even heat and less clinker. Learn to judge temperature by color: dark red is around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius, cherry red is around 800, orange is around 900, and yellow is around 1000 to 1100. For most carbon steels, forge between orange and yellow. Do not overheat to white or you will burn the steel and lose carbon. If you see sparks shooting from the steel in the fire, it is burning. Remove it immediately and discard that piece or use it for low-stress parts. Practice with a small batch of leaf spring. Cut five pieces of the same size. Forge each into a simple knife blank. Record how each piece moves under the hammer, how it hardens, and how it sharpens. This builds your intuition. Also, keep a quench tank ready. For high carbon steel, warm oil is better than water because it reduces cracking. Use old engine oil or vegetable oil. Heat it to about 50 to 60 degrees Celsius. For low carbon steel, you can quench in water, but it will not harden much. Finally, think like a business owner. Your scrap sourcing is a competitive advantage. If you can get clean, sorted, high carbon steel at a low price, you can undercut other smiths and still make a profit. Train one apprentice to sort and clean scrap while you focus on forging and selling. Set a target: for every 10 kilograms of scrap you buy, you should produce at least 6 kilograms of finished goods. The rest is waste, scale, and offcuts. Reduce waste by planning your cuts before you start. In summary, identify good steel, buy it cheaply and consistently, store it properly, prepare it safely, and forge it at the right temperature. Do these things and your quality will rise, your costs will fall, and your customers will return. In the next lesson we will cover fire management and forge design for African conditions. Before you move on, complete this exercise: collect five different types of scrap, identify each by spark test and file test, forge one small item from each, and write down the results in your notebook. Bring your notes to the next session.

lessons.title: Forge Design and Fire Management in African Workshops
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 2 of Module 9. In this lesson we build and run a forge that works in African conditions: limited electricity, variable fuel quality, and open or semi-open workshops. A good forge is not expensive; it is well designed, well maintained, and operated by a smith who understands fire. We will cover three forge types, fuel choices, air supply, fire control, and safety. First, the three common forge types. The ground forge is a shallow hole in the ground lined with clay or mud. A pipe or tuyere enters from the side to bring air. This forge is cheap and works well for charcoal. It is common in rural areas. The raised forge is a table or box made of mud, brick, or metal, with a fire pot in the center. It is easier on your back and better for long sessions. The brake drum forge is a popular African design: an old car brake drum set into a metal stand, with a tuyere pipe and a small fan or bellows. It is portable, durable, and uses less fuel because the drum concentrates heat. Choose based on your space, your fuel, and your budget. If you are just starting, build a brake drum forge. You can find a drum at any scrap yard. Cut a hole in the side for the tuyere, weld or bolt a pipe, and mount the drum on a steel frame. Add a simple hand crank blower or a small electric fan with a speed control. If electricity is unreliable, use a hand bellows made from leather and wood, or a double-chamber bellows common in West Africa. The tuyere should point slightly downward so that ash and clinker do not block it. Keep the tuyere about 5 to 10 centimeters above the bottom of the fire pot. This gives space for ash to collect and for air to spread evenly. Next, fuel. Charcoal is the most common fuel in Africa. It burns clean, lights easily, and gives good heat. But not all charcoal is equal. Hardwood charcoal from dense trees like mahogany or mvule burns hotter and longer than softwood charcoal. Buy from a reliable maker and store it dry. Wet charcoal wastes heat and creates steam. Coal is also used, especially in southern Africa. It burns hotter and longer than charcoal but produces more smoke and clinker. If you use coal, choose low-sulfur coal if possible. High-sulfur coal smells bad and damages steel. You can also use coke, which is coal with impurities burned off. Coke is clean and hot but harder to light. In some areas, you can use agricultural waste like maize cobs, coconut shells, or rice husks, but these burn fast and give uneven heat. They are best for small work or as a supplement. Whatever fuel you use, keep it dry and keep a reserve. Running out of fuel in the middle of a job is a business loss. Now, air supply. Air is the heart of the fire. Too little air and the fire is cold. Too much air and you burn steel and waste fuel. Learn to control air with a gate, a valve, or a speed control on your fan. For a hand blower, use steady, even strokes. Do not pump violently. For an electric fan, use a dimmer switch or a router speed control. A simple method is to mark your air control lever with three positions: low, medium, and high. Low for gentle heating and annealing. Medium for general forging. High for welding and heavy work. Practice changing the air as you work. When the steel is in the fire, watch the color. If the fire is too hot, the steel will spark and burn. If it is too cold, the steel will not move. Adjust air and fuel together. Fire management also means managing the shape of the fire. Build a mound of fuel around the steel. The steel should sit in the hottest part, which is just above the tuyere. Do not bury the steel deep in the fuel or it will not heat evenly. Do not leave it on top or it will not get hot enough. Rotate the steel as it heats so that all sides reach the same temperature. For a long piece, heat only the section you are working. This saves fuel and time. Learn to read the fire. A clean fire has a bright yellow-white center with a blue flame at the tuyere. A dirty fire has black smoke and a dull red center. Dirty fire means wet fuel, too much ash, or not enough air. Clean the fire by removing ash and clinker with a poker or a small shovel. Do this often. A clean fire is a hot fire. Clinker is melted ash that forms a glassy lump. It blocks air and reduces heat. Remove it as soon as you see it. In a brake drum forge, you can tilt the drum to dump ash and clinker. In a ground forge, use a hoe or a metal rake. Safety is part of fire management. Always wear leather gloves, safety glasses, and a leather apron. Do not wear synthetic clothing near the fire. Keep a bucket of water and a bucket of sand nearby. Never leave a fire unattended. At the end of the day, let the fire burn down and then quench it with water. Do not pour water on a hot forge if it is made of clay or mud; it may crack. Instead, spread the coals and let them cool. If you use coal, be aware of carbon monoxide. Work in a well-ventilated area. Do not work inside a closed room with a coal fire. For business, a well-managed fire saves money. Fuel is a major cost. If you waste fuel, you waste profit. Track your fuel use. For example, note how many kilograms of charcoal you use per knife or per hoe. Try to reduce that number by improving your fire control and your forge design. A good target is to reduce fuel use by 20 percent within three months. You can also sell your skill. Many farmers and builders need tools repaired. A portable forge lets you travel to them. Build a small cart or a wheelbarrow forge with a brake drum, a hand blower, and a bag of charcoal. Go to markets, farms, and construction sites. Charge for repairs and small fabrications. This turns your forge into a mobile business. Finally, maintain your forge. Check the tuyere for blockages. Replace worn pipes. Repair cracks in clay or mud with fresh clay. Keep the blower oiled and clean. A well-maintained forge lasts for years and gives consistent results. In the next lesson we will cover hammer techniques and basic forging processes. For now, complete this exercise: build or improve one forge using local materials, run three test fires with different air settings, and record the time it takes to heat a piece of leaf spring to orange. Bring your notes to the next session.

lessons.title: Hammer Technique and Basic Forging Processes
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 3 of Module 9. In this lesson we focus on the hammer, the anvil, and the basic processes that turn scrap steel into finished products. Good hammer technique is the difference between a smith who works all day and a smith who produces quality goods efficiently. We will cover stance, grip, hammer types, anvil setup, and the core processes: drawing, upsetting, bending, punching, cutting, and forge welding. Start with your body. Stand close to the anvil with your feet shoulder-width apart. Your hammer hand is your dominant hand. Your tong hand holds the steel. Keep your elbows slightly bent and your shoulders relaxed. Do not grip the hammer too tightly. A tight grip tires your arm and reduces control. Hold the hammer near the end of the handle for power, or closer to the head for control. For most work, hold about two-thirds of the way down the handle. Your wrist does the work, not your shoulder. Let the hammer fall with gravity. Do not force it. A heavy hammer swung with gravity does more than a light hammer swung with muscle. For most African blacksmith work, a 1 to 1.5 kilogram hammer is enough. A heavier hammer, 2 to 3 kilograms, is for heavy drawing and striking. A lighter hammer, 500 grams to 1 kilogram, is for finishing and detail. You need at least two hammers: a cross-peen and a ball-peen or a rounding hammer. The cross-peen has a wedge-shaped face for drawing out and spreading. The ball-peen has a rounded face for shaping and riveting. The flat face is for general work. Keep your hammer faces polished and slightly domed. A chipped or flat face leaves marks on the steel. Next, the anvil. A good anvil is heavy, at least 50 kilograms, and mounted at the right height. The top of the anvil should be at the height of your knuckles when you stand with your arm relaxed. If it is too high, you lose power. If it is too low, you hurt your back. Mount the anvil on a solid stump or a steel stand. Do not mount it on a loose table. A loose anvil absorbs energy and makes noise. If you do not have a traditional anvil, use a piece of railway track, a large hammer head, or a heavy steel block. Any hard, heavy steel surface works. Clean the anvil before use. Remove scale and dirt. A clean anvil gives clean work. Now the basic processes. Drawing out means making the steel longer and thinner. Heat the steel to orange or yellow. Place it on the anvil with the section you want to draw hanging over the edge. Strike with the cross-peen or the flat face at a slight angle. Work from the center outward. Do not strike the same spot repeatedly; move along the steel. This spreads the metal evenly. For heavy drawing, use a striker with a sledgehammer while you hold the steel with tongs. This is common in African workshops for making hoes, axes, and machetes. Upsetting means making the steel shorter and thicker. Heat the end of the steel to yellow. Stand it on the anvil and strike the top. The metal flows downward and thickens. This is useful for making bolt heads, tool heads, and decorative ends. Bending is simple: heat the steel to orange and bend it over the horn of the anvil or in a vise. For sharp bends, use a bending fork or a hardy hole tool. For curves, use the horn. For scrolls, use a scroll wrench or a series of bends. Punching means making a hole in the steel. Heat the steel to yellow. Place it over the hardy hole or a bolster. Use a punch made of hard steel. Strike the punch with a hammer. Turn the steel over and punch from the other side to finish the hole. This gives a clean hole without a lot of distortion. For small holes, use a drill after annealing. For large holes, punch and drift. Drifting means enlarging a punched hole with a drift pin. Cutting can be done with a hot cut or a cold chisel. A hot cut is a chisel with a long handle that fits in the hardy hole. Place the steel on the hot cut and strike it with a hammer. Turn the steel over and cut from the other side. This gives a clean cut. For cold cutting, use a hacksaw or an angle grinder. Forge welding is the most advanced basic process. It joins two pieces of steel by heating them to welding temperature and hammering them together. Welding temperature is a bright yellow to white heat, around 1200 to 1300 degrees Celsius. The steel should look like butter or wet clay. It should spark slightly. Use a flux like borax or clean sand to prevent oxidation. Bring the two pieces together quickly and hammer with light, fast blows. Start in the center and work outward. Do not hit too hard at first or you will trap scale. Forge welding takes practice. Start with low carbon steel. Once you can weld low carbon, try high carbon. In African markets, forge welding is used for making chain links, rings, and repairing tools. Practice each process with a specific goal. For example, draw a piece of leaf spring from 20 centimeters to 30 centimeters without cracking. Upset a piece from 2 centimeters to 3 centimeters in length. Punch a clean hole in a piece of flat bar. Forge weld two pieces of mild steel into a single bar. Keep a notebook and record your results. Note the temperature, the hammer, the number of heats, and the time. This data helps you improve. Also, think about production. If you make the same item many times, make a jig or a template. For example, a bending jig for hooks or a cutting guide for machetes. This reduces variation and speeds up work. Train an apprentice to do the simple tasks like cutting, cleaning, and rough drawing. You focus on the skilled work. This increases your output and your income. Safety in hammering: wear safety glasses. Hot scale flies off the steel. Wear leather gloves when handling hot steel. Keep your tongs in good condition. Do not use tongs that slip. Keep your work area clear. Do not let children or visitors stand close when you are striking. Finally, remember that hammer technique is a skill that improves with practice. Set aside 30 minutes each day for practice. Make simple items like hooks, nails, and rings. Sell them at a low price to cover your fuel. As your skill grows, move to higher value items like knives, hoes, and axes. In the next lesson we will cover heat treatment and finishing. For now, complete this exercise: forge three hooks, three nails, and one small knife from scrap steel. Record the number of heats and the time for each. Bring your notes to the next session.

lessons.title: Heat Treatment and Finishing for African Market Products
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 4 of Module 9. In this lesson we cover heat treatment and finishing. These steps turn a rough forged piece into a product that customers will pay for. In many African markets, a tool that holds an edge and looks good sells for two or three times the price of a rough tool. Heat treatment includes annealing, normalizing, hardening, and tempering. Finishing includes grinding, polishing, handle fitting, and packaging. We will go through each step with practical methods that work in a small workshop. First, annealing. Annealing softens steel so you can cut, drill, or file it. Heat the steel to a dull red, around 700 to 750 degrees Celsius. Then bury it in dry ash, sand, or vermiculite and let it cool slowly. Do not quench it. Slow cooling gives soft steel. Anneal leaf springs and files before drilling or heavy filing. Normalizing is similar but you let the steel cool in still air. Heat to orange, around 850 to 900 degrees Celsius, then take it out of the fire and let it cool in air. Normalizing refines the grain and relieves stress. Do this after heavy forging. It makes the steel stronger and less likely to crack. Hardening makes the steel hard and wear-resistant. Heat the steel to its hardening temperature. For most high carbon steels, this is a cherry red to orange color, around 780 to 850 degrees Celsius. The steel should be non-magnetic at this temperature. Test with a magnet. If the magnet does not stick, you are ready. Then quench quickly in oil or water. For high carbon steel, use warm oil. For low carbon steel, water is fine but it will not harden much. Move the steel in the quench to break the vapor jacket. Do not quench only the edge if you want the whole piece hard. For knives, you can quench the whole blade and then temper. After quenching, the steel is very hard but brittle. It can crack or chip. Tempering reduces brittleness and keeps hardness. Clean the steel to bright metal. Heat it gently to a specific color. For knives, a straw yellow to bronze color, around 200 to 250 degrees Celsius, gives a good edge. For axes and chisels, a purple to blue color, around 280 to 300 degrees Celsius, gives more toughness. You can temper in an oven, over a fire, or with a torch. Watch the color carefully. It changes fast. If you overshoot, re-harden and temper again. For African market products, heat treatment must be reliable. A farmer will not buy a second hoe if the first one bends or chips. Test your tools. Cut a piece of hardwood with a knife. Chop a small branch with an axe. Dig with a hoe. If the edge rolls, it is too soft. If it chips, it is too hard. Adjust your tempering. Keep records of your temperatures and colors. This is your quality control. Now finishing. After heat treatment, grind the piece. Use a belt grinder, an angle grinder, or a hand file. For knives, grind the bevel evenly. Do not overheat the edge. Dip in water often. For hoes and axes, grind the edge to a smooth curve. Remove all scale and rough spots. Sand with progressively finer grits: 80, 120, 220, 400. For a polished finish, go to 800 or 1000. You can polish with a cloth wheel and polishing compound. A polished blade resists rust and looks professional. For handles, choose local hardwoods like mahogany, mvule, or ebony. Dry the wood well. Shape it to fit the hand. Sand smooth. Finish with oil or wax. For knives, use a two-part epoxy or cutler's resin to glue the handle. Add rivets or pins for strength. For axes and hoes, fit the handle tightly and wedge it. Do not use soft wood. It will break and injure the user. For packaging, think about the customer. A simple cardboard sleeve with your name and phone number is enough. For higher-end knives, make a leather sheath. Leather is available in many African markets. Cut, stitch, and wet-form the sheath to the blade. Add a belt loop. This adds value and protects the customer. For pricing, calculate your costs: steel, fuel, grinding wheels, sandpaper, handle material, packaging, and your time. Add a profit margin of at least 30 percent. Do not compete only on price. Compete on quality and service. Offer a guarantee. If a tool breaks within one month of normal use, repair or replace it. This builds trust. Also, diversify your products. In addition to knives and hoes, make: garden tools like trowels and weeders; kitchen tools like cleavers and spoons; construction tools like chisels and punches; decorative items like wall hooks and bottle openers. Each product has a different market. Test small batches at local markets. Ask customers what they need. Adjust your designs. For example, in some areas, farmers prefer a short handle for weeding. In others, they prefer a long handle. Make both. For finishing, pay attention to detail. A sharp edge, a smooth handle, and a clean finish show that you care. Customers notice. Word of mouth is your best marketing. One satisfied customer brings three more. Finally, keep your workshop clean. Sweep the floor. Organize your tools. Store finished goods in a dry place. Rust is your enemy. Oil your products before storage. Use a light coat of vegetable oil or machine oil. For long storage, wrap in paper or cloth. In the next lesson we will cover pricing, marketing, and business growth. For now, complete this exercise: take one forged knife and one forged hoe through the full heat treatment and finishing process. Test them. Record the colors, the quench medium, the tempering temperature, and the final performance. Bring your notes and your finished products to the next session.

lessons.title: Pricing, Marketing, and Growing Your Blacksmith Business
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 5 of Module 9. In this final lesson we focus on the business side of blacksmithing. You can be the best smith in your area, but if you cannot price, market, and manage money, you will struggle. We will cover costing, pricing, marketing, sales, customer service, record keeping, and growth. Start with costing. You must know the true cost of every item you make. List all costs: raw material, fuel, consumables like grinding wheels and sandpaper, handle material, packaging, transport, rent, electricity, and labor. Include your own time. If you do not pay yourself, you are not running a business. For example, if a knife uses 1 kilogram of scrap steel at 2 dollars, 3 dollars of charcoal, 1 dollar of sandpaper and grinding, 2 dollars of handle material, and 1 dollar of packaging, your direct cost is 9 dollars. If it takes you 2 hours and you value your time at 5 dollars per hour, your total cost is 19 dollars. Add a profit margin of 30 percent. Your selling price should be at least 25 dollars. If the market will not pay that, you must reduce costs or increase efficiency. Maybe you can buy steel in bulk for 1.50 dollars per kilogram. Maybe you can make two knives in the same time. Maybe you can use a cheaper handle material. Do the math. Do not guess. Next, pricing strategy. There are three common approaches: cost-plus, market-based, and value-based. Cost-plus is what we just did. Market-based means you check what others charge and set your price near theirs. Value-based means you charge based on what the customer saves or earns. For example, a farmer who uses your hoe to grow more maize can earn an extra 100 dollars per season. Your hoe at 30 dollars is a good value. Use value-based pricing for high-quality tools. Use cost-plus for simple items. Offer different grades: a basic model, a standard model, and a premium model. This lets customers choose. For marketing, start with your current customers. Ask them for referrals. Give a small discount for every new customer they bring. Put a sign on your workshop. Use bright paint. Show your products. Keep the area clean. At markets, display your best work. Demonstrate your skills. Sharpen a knife for free. This attracts a crowd. Use word of mouth. In many African communities, trust is built through personal relationships. Join a local business association or a cooperative. Share orders with other smiths when you are busy. They will return the favor. Use mobile phones. Take photos of your products. Share them on WhatsApp, Facebook, or Instagram. Create a simple catalog with prices. Send it to potential customers like hardware stores, agricultural supply shops, and hotels. Offer wholesale prices for bulk orders. For sales, be professional. Greet customers warmly. Ask about their needs. Do not just sell a product; solve a problem. If a farmer needs a hoe for rocky soil, recommend a heavier blade. If a chef needs a knife for fish, recommend a flexible blade. Follow up after the sale. Ask if the tool is working well. This builds loyalty. For customer service, offer a guarantee. Repair or replace defective products. Keep your promises. Deliver on time. If you cannot meet a deadline, communicate early. A customer who is informed is more forgiving than one who is ignored. For record keeping, use a simple notebook or a mobile app. Record every sale: date, item, quantity, price, customer name, and payment method. Record every expense. At the end of each month, calculate your profit. Separate your business money from your personal money. Open a bank account or a mobile money account for the business. Save at least 10 percent of your profit for equipment and emergencies. Pay yourself a regular salary. This helps you plan. For growth, consider these steps. First, increase production. Train apprentices. Assign them repetitive tasks. Pay them fairly. Second, diversify products. Add new items based on customer demand. Third, expand your market. Sell to neighboring towns, schools, hotels, and NGOs. Fourth, improve quality. Invest in better tools: a belt grinder, a drill press, a welder. Fifth, formalize your business. Register it. Pay taxes. This opens doors to larger contracts. Sixth, build a brand. Choose a name and a logo. Use it on all products and packaging. Be consistent. Finally, think about the future. Blacksmithing is an ancient trade, but it is not dying. It is changing. There is growing demand for handmade, locally made goods. Tourists and urban customers pay premium prices for authentic African knives, tools, and art. You can also teach. Offer short courses to hobbyists and students. This adds income and builds your reputation. In summary, run your blacksmith shop like a business. Know your costs. Price for profit. Market consistently. Serve customers well. Keep records. Save and reinvest. Grow step by step. You have the skills. Now you need the discipline. For your final exercise, create a one-page business plan for the next three months. Include your products, prices, target customers, marketing activities, and profit goal. Bring it to the next session for review. Congratulations on completing Module 9. You are now equipped to source, forge, finish, and sell quality blacksmith products in your community. Keep your fire hot, your hammer true, and your accounts balanced. Your business will grow.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Blacksmith Workshop Safety, Tooling Standards, and Production Records for African Forges

This practical reference lesson consolidates the technical, safety, and business records that a working African blacksmith needs to run a forge profitably. It is designed as a bench-side companion to Modules 1â8 of the RISE AFRICA "Yok and Pan Blacksmith" course. The focus is on three things that separate a subsistence smith from a commercially viable one: safe and efficient workshop practice, standardised tool and product specifications, and simple record-keeping that supports pricing, credit, and repeat sales.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, blacksmithing remains a viable rural enterprise. The FAO reports that small-scale metalworking and tool production is a critical rural non-farm activity supporting agricultural value chains, particularly for hand tools such as hoes, machetes, and axes. A smith who can produce a consistent, well-tempered hoe blade to a known specification can supply cooperatives, agro-dealers, and NGOs â not just walk-in customers. That shift from retail to contract supply is where the real money is, and it demands the discipline described below.

1. Workshop Layout and Workflow Standards

The diagram above shows the standard three-point forge arrangement: hearth, anvil, and quench trough within a one- to two-step reach. This layout is not cosmetic. It reduces the time a hot workpiece is out of the fire, which reduces heat loss, re-heating costs, and fuel consumption. In charcoal-fired forges, fuel is often the single largest recurring cost â typically 20â35% of production cost for a hoe or machete blade. Layout efficiency translates directly into margin.

Position the anvil so the smith faces the hearth at roughly 90 degrees. This allows the left hand to hold tongs at the fire while the right hand hammers, with a single pivot to the anvil. The quench trough should be on the opposite side of the anvil from the fire, so a hot blade never passes over the fuel bed. The tool rack belongs within arm's reach of the anvil, not the fire.

2. Tooling and Product Specifications

Buyers â especially cooperatives, agro-dealers, and NGOs â increasingly require standardised dimensions. A hoe that weighs 700 g in one batch and 950 g in the next breaks trust. Table 1 gives reference specifications for common African market tools, compiled from FAO and university extension guidance on small-scale agricultural tool production. Use these as a starting point and adjust to your local market, but keep the specification fixed once agreed with a buyer.

3. Fuel, Consumables, and Cost Tracking

Most African forges run on charcoal, with some using coal, coke, or agricultural residues. Fuel efficiency is the single biggest lever on unit cost. Table 2 shows approximate fuel consumption benchmarks for a typical forge producing hand tools. Track your own figures monthly â a smith who does not know their fuel cost per hoe cannot price profitably.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Health and Chemical Hazards in the Forge

Forging and finishing generate serious health risks. Metal fume fever from welding or galvanised scrap (zinc) causes flu-like symptoms; never forge galvanised or painted steel without forced ventilation and a P2/P3 respirator. Silica dust from grinding and sanding can cause silicosis â always wear eye protection and a dust mask. Waste engine oil used for quenching contains carcinogenic PAHs; use in a well-ventilated area, avoid skin contact, and never use it for food-contact items. Charcoal and coal fires produce carbon monoxide â never work in a closed room. Burns and eye injuries are the most common forge accidents; keep a first-aid kit and clean water on site at all times. WHO guidance on occupational health in informal metalworking recommends mandatory eye and respiratory protection, and annual health checks for full-time smiths.

4. Record-Keeping for Pricing, Credit, and Growth

You do not need a computer. A single exercise book with four columns per sale â date, product, quantity, price, and cost â is enough to run a profitable forge. The purpose is threefold: (1) know your true unit cost, (2) prove reliability to contract buyers, and (3) access credit or savings groups with evidence of turnover.

At minimum, record weekly: fuel purchased, scrap purchased, tools produced, tools sold, cash received, cash owed to you (credit sales), and cash you owe (supplier credit). Review monthly. If your fuel cost per tool is rising, check for heat-loss waste, poor forge design, or wet fuel. If your credit sales exceed 20% of turnover, tighten terms â informal credit is the most common cause of forge cash-flow failure.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  • Layout: Hearth, anvil, and quench within one to two steps; tool rack at the anvil, not the fire.
  • Ventilation: Open sides or roof vent; never work in a closed room with charcoal or coal.
  • PPE: Eye protection, leather gloves, apron, closed boots, and dust mask for grinding â every session.
  • Specification: Fix blade mass, length, and edge hardness for each product; keep a physical sample for reference.
  • Fuel: Weigh or count charcoal per batch for one week each month; investigate any rise above baseline.
  • Quench: Use clean water or dedicated quenching oil; never use waste oil on food-contact items.
  • Records: Log every sale and every purchase; review fuel cost per tool monthly.
  • Credit: Keep credit sales below 20% of turnover; write down every debtor and due date.
  • Health: Annual check for eyes, lungs, and skin; report persistent cough or eye irritation early.

Business takeaway: A forge that runs on a fixed specification, tracked fuel cost, and a written sales record can quote confidently to cooperatives and NGOs, absorb credit sales without collapsing, and reinvest in better tooling. That is the difference between a smith who works and a smith who earns.

quiz.q: In Module 9 of Yok and Pan Blacksmith training, what is the primary purpose of the tempering stage after hardening?
options: A) To increase brittleness for edge retention
B) To reduce internal stresses and toughen the steel
C) To change the steel color to blue permanently
D) To remove all carbon from the surface
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces internal stresses and toughens the steel after hardening, balancing hardness with durability.

quiz.q: Which quenching medium is generally considered the fastest cooling rate in blacksmithing?
options: A) Air
B) Oil
C) Brine
D) Sand
quiz.explanation: Brine cools faster than oil, air, or sand, producing a very rapid quench that can increase hardness but also risk cracking.

quiz.q: What visual indicator is commonly used to judge tempering temperature in traditional blacksmithing?
options: A) Spark pattern
B) Magnetism
C) Oxide colors
D) Sound of the hammer
quiz.explanation: Oxide colors on polished steel indicate tempering temperature ranges, such as straw, brown, purple, and blue.

quiz.q: Why should a blacksmith normalize a forged piece before hardening?
options: A) To make it magnetic
B) To add a decorative finish
C) To increase carbon content
D) To refine grain structure and relieve stress
quiz.explanation: Normalizing refines grain structure and relieves stresses from forging, leading to more predictable hardening results.

quiz.q: What happens if steel is quenched below its critical temperature?
options: A) It will not fully harden
B) It will become too soft to grind
C) It will automatically temper itself
D) It will turn into wrought iron
quiz.explanation: If steel is quenched below critical temperature, the austenite does not fully transform, so it will not reach full hardness.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects the hardenability of steel?
options: A) Hammer weight
B) Alloy composition
C) Forge color
D) Anvil height
quiz.explanation: Hardenability is primarily determined by alloy composition, especially carbon and other alloying elements.

quiz.q: What is a common sign that a piece should be tempered immediately after quenching?
options: A) It is still glowing red
B) It has a rough scale
C) It is hard and brittle
D) It is cold to the touch
quiz.explanation: After quenching, steel is hard and brittle, so tempering should follow promptly to reduce brittleness.

quiz.q: In blacksmithing, what does the term critical temperature refer to?
options: A) The temperature at which steel melts completely
B) The temperature at which steel becomes nonmagnetic and phase change occurs
C) The temperature at which oil ignites
D) The temperature at which the forge reaches maximum heat
quiz.explanation: Critical temperature is the point where steel changes phase and becomes nonmagnetic, important for hardening and normalizing.
